name: Roter Eiserapfel
history: One of the oldest German apples, thought to come from Franconia and grown around Bamberg and Nuremberg by the 16th-17th centuries; it gathered dozens of local names across central Europe. Famous as a phenomenal keeper, it was the traditional Christmas and Krampus apple in parts of Germany and Austria. The UK National Fruit Collection holds it as a triploid.

look.description: Lopsided, slightly ribbed fruit washed dark blood-red with a bluish bloom and many pale lenticel dots.

taste.summary: Very firm, fine-grained cream flesh, juicy once mellowed. Sweet with a gentle subacid balance but little aroma and a faintly astringent edge; it needs several weeks in store to reach full flavour.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Apr; at its best after 4-6 weeks in store, keeping into summer in a cool cellar

tree.notes: Strong, long-lived tree making a very broad crown; a traditional orchard (Streuobst) standard. Undemanding and healthy.

pollination.notes: Triploid: needs two diploid partners and is a poor pollen donor. Blossom is late and long-lasting and stands up well to poor weather. Group estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates (full bloom mid May).

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist central European uplands and similar damp temperate regions, including heavy, not very fertile soils.
climate.poor_climates: Warm valley sites and hot, dry summers, which German growers regard as unsuitable.

health.other: Regarded as very healthy; only minor susceptibility to canker and fire blight is reported.

grow_notes: Best as a large standard or half-standard on heavier, moisture-retentive soil, where it will live for generations. Plant two diploid pollinators that flower mid-to-late season. Pick in October and store cool; it improves for weeks before eating.

name: Rouville
history: Released by Agriculture Canada in 1983 from the apple breeding programme that moved from Ottawa to Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Quebec, in 1971 with aims of scab resistance and juice and cider quality. It is a hardy, scab-resistant summer apple; its parentage is not published in the sources consulted.

look.description: Flattish apple, largely flushed deep red over a pale greenish-yellow ground.

taste.summary: Very juicy, somewhat coarse flesh with a sweet, subacid flavour that growers liken to berries, finished by a light but noticeable tannic grip that suits juice and cider.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-Sep from the tree; keeps about two months chilled

tree.notes: Vigorous and very productive according to growers.

pollination.notes: No UK flowering group recorded; plant with another mid-season diploid.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter, humid regions such as southern Quebec and the Maritimes, where its scab immunity saves spraying.
climate.poor_climates: Hot-summer regions, where an early apple of this type softens quickly; untested in low-chill areas.

health.other: Bred for scab resistance and reported immune to the common North American scab races; other disease behaviour not documented.

grow_notes: A good low-spray choice for cold, wet districts. Pick over a short window as it ripens, and use quickly for eating, juicing or blending into cider.

name: Sandow
history: Selected in 1912 at the Central Experimental Farm in Ottawa from seedlings of Northern Spy and introduced in 1935. It was valued as a hardier, earlier-bearing and less scab-prone alternative to its parent; a tetraploid form (Hunter Sandow) is also held at the UK National Fruit Collection.

look.description: Large, flattish apple streaked bright scarlet over a red flush on a green-yellow ground.

taste.summary: Juicy cream flesh, crisp at first and becoming tender, with a balanced sweet-sharp flavour and a light raspberry note noted by several growers.

tree.notes: Comes into bearing sooner than Northern Spy. A tetraploid sport, Hunter Sandow, exists.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates (full bloom around 12 May).

climate.best_climates: Cold continental regions of eastern Canada and the northern US (reported for zones 3-5), and cool temperate gardens.
climate.poor_climates: Hot southern summers and mild-winter areas lacking chill.

health.other: Described as more scab resistant than Northern Spy; other disease data lacking.

grow_notes: A hardy late keeper for cold districts that wants the flavour of Northern Spy without the long wait for crops. Pick in October and store until winter.

name: Shinsei
history: Raised in 1930 at the Aomori Apple Experiment Station in northern Japan and named in 1948. It belongs to the early wave of Japanese crosses using Golden Delicious.

look.description: Pale greenish to whitish-yellow apple with a faint pink cheek, looking like a small Golden Delicious.

taste.summary: White, fine-grained flesh, crisp and juicy when fresh, with a very sweet, low-acid and lightly scented flavour; it softens within a few weeks of picking.

tree.notes: National Fruit Collection records a drooping tree habit.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates (full bloom around 12 May).

climate.best_climates: Temperate regions with warm summers and cold winters, like its home in northern Honshu.
climate.poor_climates: Very hot or mild-winter regions, and short cool summers; not documented outside collections.

grow_notes: A collector's apple rather than a garden standard. Pick in late September and eat within a few weeks, before the low-acid flesh turns soft.

name: Sinta

origin.raised_by: K.O. Lapins, Canada Department of Agriculture, Summerland

history: Raised in 1955 by K.O. Lapins at the Canadian research station in Summerland, British Columbia, from a cross of Golden Delicious with its probable parent Grimes Golden. It was released for trial in the 1960s but never became widespread.

look.description: Pale yellow, sometimes almost cream-white apple with a slight pinkish-orange cheek where sunned.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy, deep-cream flesh with a sweet, aromatic flavour that growers rate above both parents; a little crunchier than Golden Delicious.

tree.notes: National Fruit Collection records a spreading to drooping habit.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates (full bloom around 10 May).

climate.best_climates: Warm-summer temperate regions such as interior British Columbia and similar fruit districts.
climate.poor_climates: Very cold winters and short cool summers that may not ripen it; humid areas if, like its parents, it is prone to disease (not documented).

grow_notes: A good choice for anyone who likes Golden Delicious but wants more aroma. Pick in early-to-mid October; it keeps until around the New Year in a cool store.

name: Snövit
history: Raised in 1936 by Emil Johansson at Alnarp in southern Sweden; the name means Snow White and refers to its strikingly white flesh. It is a Swedish summer apple suited to both eating and cooking.

look.description: Conical, whitish-yellow apple striped with red.

taste.summary: Very soft, snow-white flesh sometimes tinged pink, with a sweet and lightly perfumed flavour balanced by moderate acidity. It is not very juicy and goes over quickly.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-Sep, within a few weeks of picking

tree.notes: Early to flower. National Fruit Collection records a spreading to drooping habit.

pollination.notes: Early flowering; Swedish sources list partners such as James Grieve, Melba, Transparente Blanche, Sävstaholm and Gyllenkroks Astrakan. Group estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates (full bloom around 6 May).

climate.best_climates: Cool Scandinavian and northern European climates; grown in Swedish zones III-V.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers, where an early soft apple turns mealy fast; humid areas because of scab.

health.other: Swedish sources flag susceptibility to scab.

grow_notes: A hardy summer apple for cold gardens. Pick when the first fruits colour and eat promptly, as it keeps only a few weeks. Choose an airy site to limit scab.

name: Spigold

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Red Spy x Golden Delicious (the NFC records the Red Spy parent as Rodluvan)
origin.raised_by: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva

history: Introduced in 1962 by the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva from a cross of a red Northern Spy sport with Golden Delicious. A large triploid dessert apple, it is grown mainly by amateurs and enthusiasts who prize its flavour.

look.description: Big conical apple about three-quarters striped bright red over golden yellow, with a tender skin.

taste.summary: Fine-grained, firm, crisp and very juicy yellow flesh with a sprightly sweet flavour; tasters report honeyed and citrus-like notes, though collection tasters found the aroma modest.

tree.notes: Large, fairly vigorous tree with a tendency to crop biennially. Triploid, so it gives little useful pollen.

pollination.notes: Triploid: needs two diploid partners in group 3-5 and will not pollinate them back.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter temperate regions such as New York and the Great Lakes, and mild damp maritime climates.
climate.poor_climates: Hot humid areas where cedar-apple rust is common, and mild-winter regions lacking chill.

health.other: Very susceptible to cedar-apple rust; some fire blight resistance. Tender skin bruises easily.

grow_notes: Give it space and two good diploid pollinators. Thin in heavy years to even out biennial cropping, and handle the fruit gently at picking.

name: Star of Devon
history: Raised by J. Garland at Broadclyst near Exeter and introduced by George Pyne's Denver Nurseries in Topsham; it received an RHS Award of Merit in 1905. It is a parent of Cheddar Cross and has been grown on the Killerton estate near Broadclyst.

look.description: Medium apple heavily striped red over yellow, with a slightly greasy skin.

taste.summary: Soft, greenish-white flesh with a rather sharp flavour and only a faint aroma.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates (full bloom around 9 May).

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp south-west England and similar maritime climates where it was raised.
climate.poor_climates: Hot or very cold continental climates; no documented performance outside Britain.

grow_notes: A Devon heritage apple mainly of local interest. Pick in mid October and store; it keeps through winter.
